text: Next version 'vmix' is coded, tested and signed. Its memory first reads real past frames, then also frames the model drew itself. Its cache of drawn frames had to be redrawn one frame at a time (drawing 8 at once changed the numbers slightly); the redraw matches exactly and finishes around 07:00. Meanwhile the big GPU trains the matching comparison version. Speed: merging the fine-tuning weights made frames ~2x faster (1.6 s at 25 steps, 0.3 s at 4 steps; goal 0.1 s).

Private-noise version stopped at 12k under the pre-agreed rule (two safety misses in a row): car accuracy and the picture difference to the key were over their limits at 8k and 12k (mostly a constant offset, not growing drift). Smoothness at 12k was its best (15% fewer car jumps and 7% less wobble than A; the bar is 9.4% on both), but it did not improve at every check. The next design's first test also missed, so the council is designing round 2.

Private-noise version at 8k (the first check that counts): car jumps are 10% below A, but wobble is level with A, and car accuracy and drift both crossed their safety limits, with more fake cars lingering (18 vs 4 per drive). One more safety miss at 12k stops this version. The next design (memory that reads the finished picture of past frames) is coded and passing its first tests.

First look at the private-noise version (2k steps, look-only): it is already a bit LESS jumpy than A on car jumps (-9%) and 27% less jumpy than its own memory-off version, where the first live model was 62% jumpier than A at the same point. The catch: car accuracy is near its limit and more fake cars linger. The checks that count start at 8k.

The private-noise version started training after all tests passed and Astra signed the launch code (on the sixth review; each earlier one found a real hole). It trains to 12k, pauses while 12k is scored, and continues to 16k only if the safety bars allow.

The first live video model finished 16,000 steps: it was jumpier than A at every check (16k: +58% car jumps, +15% wobble), so it did not pass. Car accuracy stayed just inside its limit and drift was near zero. That triggers the fix agreed in advance: train it again with private noise for every frame.

Change of plan: we were spending most GPU time on drawing and grading test videos and too little on training (training was about 13%). Now: ONE memory version trained long (about 20k steps) next to a no-memory version of the same length, quick checks every 5k steps with a side-by-side video, and one full exam at the end. The two AI reviewers pick which version. The car map is parked, not dead: it only ever got 1-2k steps.

Memory version C (trained partly on its own output) is the best so far on the practice drives: 12-19% fewer car jumps, 9-11% less wobble, car placement and drift fine. Its only weak point is a few lingering fake cars (+4 to +6 per drive; B had +8 to +14), which we will deal with later. The reviewers now pick the one version to train long.

Plan for today: the jumpy video comes first. The memory versions are being judged on 30 test drives (verdict aimed for midday). Version B cuts jumps by about 10-20% but leaves fake cars lingering, so it fails the safety checks; version C is being scored. The car map is closed. The two AI reviewers are planning the next video step (e.g. a model that draws several frames together) in case B and C are not enough.

Car map, last try (map fed in at four depths): it now does use the map (car-area error 3-4% lower with the right map), but the right map beats a wrong one on only 2/3 of frames; the plan needed 3/4. Per the rule both reviewers signed beforehand, the car-map track is closed. The final model will be E3 plus the best memory version.

Car map, second design: still not using the map enough. With the right map vs a wrong map, the model's guess at car areas is better only 54-59% of the time (needed 75%). Early stop per plan; the reviewers decide whether to try the last named fallback.

Steady video, first verdict on 30 test drives: the no-training trick (start each frame from the last one) cuts car flicker by 23% but places cars worse (0.26 vs 0.32), drifts over 15 s and leaves lingering phantom cars (13.7 vs 5.1 per drive). It fails the plan's checks, so it is not used. Next: the three trained memory versions.

Car map redesign signed by both AI reviewers: feed the car boxes straight into the model's first layer, reward getting the car pixels right, and hide the cameras half the time early on so the model has to use the map. Two bugs fixed first: detector car angles were mirrored, and the detector used lidar-based car positions (now camera calibration only).

Car map re-tested with the bug fixed: the map now changes the picture, but the right map and a wrong map change it the same way (car score 0.315 vs 0.323; base model 0.318). So the add-on still does not use where the cars are. Early stop, valid this time; the two AI reviewers are redesigning it.

Correction: the 'car map is ignored' result was our bug, caught by the hourly AI review. The drawing script gave the car map to only the first of 25 drawing steps. Fixed; the halfway car-map test is being re-run. The steady-video scorer was also fixed to weight every drive equally before anything is ranked.

Car map halfway check: the model ignores the map. With the right map, a wrong map, or no map, the pictures come out almost the same (car score 0.325 vs 0.321 vs 0.318). The plan's early stop fired for both versions; the design goes back to the two AI reviewers with a diagnosis.

Car map check: the borrowed car detector is better on drives it was trained on (finds 85% of cars vs 72% on unseen drives). So the training car maps were roughened (drop some boxes, nudge some, add a few fake ones, by distance) until they match unseen drives: 94/79/51% found near/mid/far vs 95/79/51%. Car map runs X1 and X2 submitted; memory test rollouts started.

Added the plan from here: one base model (E3), two add-ons (memory for steady video, a car map for car placement), each with a pass test and rough times. Aim: a final model checked on 24 untouched drives by about 28 Nov.

Two research plans signed off by both AI reviewers: steadier video (feed the model its previous frame, judged on edge-car flicker) and a car map (draw a camera-only 3D detector's boxes into the chase view so cars land in the right place). Both start from E3 and run in parallel.

Where do the cars go wrong? A separate camera-only 3D detector (BEVFormer) finds the cars almost as well as the true labels do (0.42 vs 0.46 with the same box method), while our renderer reaches 42% of what it could. So the cameras do contain the positions; our model loses them on the way. Feeding the renderer the detector's 3D view is the next idea for placement.

10,000-step scores: a quarter of the data (E3, car score 0.32) does as well as all of it (E1, 0.29), so more data would not help yet. The perfect game picture through the same image compression scores 0.76, so we are at about 42% of what the judge can measure.

First scores at 5,000 steps on 30 unseen drives. Starting from plain Stable Diffusion (E2) places almost no cars correctly (car score 0.04), so we stopped it. A quarter of the data (E3) already scores 0.29, a bit lower than on its own training drives (0.36). E1 is still being scored.

Next experiment planned: steadier video. Two AI reviewers agreed a plan after five rounds: feed the model its previous frame, compared against free tricks, judged on edge-car flicker without losing placement.

First pictures at 2,500 steps. Starting from our trained model (E1), the drawings already match the game view closely: road shape, crossings, rows of parked cars, trucks ahead. Plain Stable Diffusion (E2) invents cones and misplaces cars. Fed another street's cameras, E1 draws a different street, so it reads the cameras.
Three experiments started: our trained model vs plain Stable Diffusion as the starting point, and all drives vs a quarter of them.
12,111 game pictures rendered from the chase camera (9,587 for training, 2,524 from drives the model never sees). Two cluster machines froze the simulator on every drive; we stopped using them.
New direction. Our answer keys were always messy, and the model copied the mess. Now the answer is a game render of the exact same moment, seen from behind our car.
The Stable Diffusion renderer finished 40,000 steps on the old, messy keys: photo-like streets, but car placement stopped improving after 20,000 steps.
